The Pinpoint lampfish (Lampanyctus regalis) is a mesopelagic myctophid that undergoes a dramatic ontogenetic shift from a planktonic larval phase to a vertically migrating adult. During its early life history, the species begins as a yolk-sac larva that relies entirely on endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, is approximately 0.000014 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000014 grams], a figure derived from the estimated egg diameter of 0.3 millimeters. This remarkably small initial mass is typical of teleosts that produce numerous pelagic eggs, reflecting a strategy of high fecundity offset by minimal per-offspring investment. Following a brief lecithotrophic phase, the larvae commence active feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth. This accelerated growth trajectory is sustained throughout the pelagic larval period, preparing the individual for the morphological transformation that accompanies larval metamorphosis and subsequent settlement into the juvenile stage.

As the juvenile fish grow and approach the transition to sexual maturation, a key milestone is the attainment of the standard length at which puberty is initiated. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies indicate that the standard length at puberty is 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters], a measurement that marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. This body length is a critical life-history threshold, as it represents the point at which individuals begin to allocate resources toward reproductive development rather than exclusively toward somatic growth. The wet weight at puberty, approximately 26 grams [Wwp = approximately 26 grams], is closely associated with this length, providing a more comprehensive measure of the energetic reserves available at the onset of maturity. Juveniles below this size are considered immature and do not yet participate in the annual spawning aggregations characteristic of the species. This pattern of size-based maturation is common among mesopelagic fishes, where body size often dictates reproductive competence.

Reproductive output in the Pinpoint lampfish is notably high, reflecting a life-history strategy adapted to the relatively low productivity of the mesopelagic environment. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of their habitat, which average 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], sexually mature females achieve a substantial daily reproductive output. The maximum reproductive rate observed at this temperature is estimated from the product of fecundity per spawning event and spawning frequency. Specifically, individual females produce approximately 1,233 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,233 eggs per spawning event] and typically complete one spawning event per year [F_R_i = one spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive effort results in a total yearly fecundity that allows the species to maintain stable populations despite high rates of egg and larval mortality in the open ocean. The combination of relatively large clutch sizes and an iteroparous reproductive schedule is consistent with the patterns seen in other myctophid species.

The ultimate body size achieved by Lampanyctus regalis is an important determinant of its ecological role and life-history trajectory. The maximum recorded standard length for this species is 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], representing the asymptotic limit of somatic growth. Corresponding to this length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual is approximately 95 grams [Wwi = approximately 95 grams], which represents the maximal body mass attained after growth has essentially ceased. This relationship between length and weight is consistent with the allometric scaling equation typical for teleost fishes, where weight increases as a power function of length. Attaining this ultimate size requires several years of sustained feeding and growth in the cold, deep-water environment the species inhabits. Individuals that reach this size are typically among the oldest and most reproductively successful members of the population, having accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support repeated spawning events over their lifespan. The relatively modest maximum size of this myctophid, compared to some epipelagic predators, reflects the energetic constraints of life in a low-temperature, low-food environment.

Longevity in the Pinpoint lampfish is closely tied to the cold thermal regime of its mesopelagic habitat. The maximum lifespan, recorded under the stable temperature conditions of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], is approximately six years [am = approximately six years], a duration that positions the species among the longer-lived members of its family. This lifespan is calculated from the total number of days lived, which is equivalent to roughly 2,190 days [am = roughly 2,190 days] when expressed on a daily t at a temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]imescale. Extended longevity in cold-water fishes is often linked to reduced metabolic rates and slower rates of cellular senescence, which allow individuals to maintain physiological function over many years. For a fish that reaches reproductive maturity at a standard length of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters] and a wet weight of 26 grams [Wwp = 26 grams], a six-year lifespan provides ample opportunity for multiple reproductive cycles. The ultimate wet weight of 95 grams [Wwi = 95 grams] and the ultimate length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters] are typically approached only in the final years of life, once growth has decelerated. This life-history pattern—slow growth, late maturation, and long lifespan—is a classic example of the energetically conservative strategy favored in deep-sea environments.
